title: Mid-Term ICSE Class 10 Maths: What It Covers & How to Prepare (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Mid-Term ICSE Class 10 Maths: Syllabus & Prep
meta_desc: What the mid-term ICSE Class 10 maths paper covers, unit by unit, plus the exact paper pattern and a smart 6-week prep plan. Try the free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: By September the ICSE Class 10 maths mid-term lands, and it usually pulls from the front half of the syllabus — GST, banking, shares, quadratics, inequations. Here is exactly what to expect and how to prepare, with a quick quiz to test yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The mid-term ICSE Class 10 maths paper usually lands somewhere between the last week of September and mid-October, and it catches a lot of students off guard for one simple reason: it is not a soft internal test. Most CISCE-affiliated schools set it as a proper two-and-a-half-hour, 80-mark paper on the same pattern as the March board exam, drawn from whatever the class has finished by then. If you treat it like a quiz, it bites. If you treat it like a board rehearsal, it becomes the single most useful practice run you get all year.

I have watched students score 20 marks higher in the finals simply because the mid-term forced them to sit through a full paper once, under time pressure, before it mattered. So the goal here is not just to pass it — it is to use it. Below is what the mid-term ICSE Class 10 maths syllabus typically covers, how the paper is built, and a six-week plan that actually fits around school.

What the mid-term ICSE Class 10 maths syllabus covers

Schools vary, but by September the front half of the CISCE Class 10 syllabus is usually done, and that is what the mid-term draws from. Expect the commercial and algebra-heavy units first — they are taught early and they carry a lot of marks.

  • GST (Goods and Services Tax) — the topic that replaced the old sales-tax and VAT chapter. Intra-state (CGST + SGST) versus inter-state (IGST), input tax credit, and the final price to the consumer. Almost guaranteed to appear.
  • Banking — recurring deposit accounts. You compute the maturity value using the ₹ monthly deposit, the rate, and the equivalent-months formula. Small chapter, reliable marks.
  • Shares and Dividends — nominal (face) value versus market value, dividend income, percentage yield, and how many shares a given investment buys.
  • Linear Inequations — solving in one variable, the sign-flip rule when you multiply or divide by a negative, and representing the solution on a number line over a stated set like the integers or whole numbers.
  • Quadratic Equations — solving by factorisation and by the quadratic formula, the nature of roots via the discriminant, and word problems that reduce to a quadratic (age, speed-distance, geometry).
  • Ratio and Proportion — continued proportion, mean proportional, and the properties (componendo and dividendo) that turn ugly-looking equations into one clean step.
  • Matrices — order of a matrix, addition and subtraction, scalar and matrix multiplication, and simple equations where you solve for unknown entries.

Some schools push a bit further into Arithmetic and Geometric Progressions or the early coordinate-geometry work on the section and distance formulae. Check the exact portion your school circulated — that notice is the real syllabus, not this list.

The ICSE Class 10 maths paper pattern

The mid-term almost always mirrors the board blueprint, so getting comfortable with the shape now pays off in March. The paper is 80 marks, two and a half hours, with the first fifteen minutes given only for reading — use them, do not start writing.

SectionMarksStructureChoice
Section A40Compulsory short questions, often including an MCQ setNone — attempt all
Section B40Longer questions, usually 7 of them worth about 5 or 6 marks eachAttempt any 4 of the 7

The choice in Section B is the part students misread most. You do not answer all seven — you pick your strongest four. That single habit, deciding in the reading time which four to commit to, is worth practising before the real thing.

How to prepare: a six-week plan

The honest truth about ICSE maths is that it rewards method marks. The board pays for correct working even when the final answer slips, so writing every step — formula, substitution, simplification — is not neatness, it is strategy. Here is how I would spread the six weeks before a mid-term.

Weeks 1–2: rebuild the commercial maths

Start with GST, banking, and shares. They are formula-driven and quick to bank. Do not just read the worked example — redo it with the book closed. For shares, the classic trap is confusing the ₹ nominal value (used for dividends) with the market value (used for what you actually pay); get that distinction cold and half the errors vanish.

Weeks 3–4: the algebra core

Quadratics, inequations, and ratio-proportion are where the harder marks live. For quadratics, always check the discriminant first when a question asks about the nature of roots — students lose easy marks solving for roots that were never wanted. For inequations, the negative-sign flip is the single most common slip in the whole paper. Write it on a sticky note.

Weeks 5–6: matrices, mixed practice, and full papers

Finish matrices (short and scoring), then switch entirely to solving past mid-term and board papers against the clock. Aim for at least three full 80-mark papers under real timing. Mark them harshly using the official marking scheme so you learn where method marks are actually awarded.

Common mistakes that cost marks

  • Solving all seven questions in Section B and running out of time on the ones that counted.
  • Skipping working to ‘save time’ and losing the method marks the answer would have earned.
  • Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when dividing by a negative number.
  • Rounding money to the wrong number of decimal places in GST and RD problems.
  • Mixing up nominal and market value in shares and dividends.

Try the mid-term quiz below

Below is a free eight-question quiz drawn from exactly these units — GST, banking, shares, inequations, quadratics, ratio, and matrices — pitched at ICSE Class 10 level. Attempt each one, then read the explanation for anything you miss. When you are ready for longer written practice, the graded chapter worksheets and full mock papers linked below give you plenty to work through with answer keys.

quiz.title: Mid-Term ICSE Class 10 Maths Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions across GST, banking, shares, inequations, quadratics, ratio and matrices — the core of the ICSE mid-term. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: For an intra-state sale, GST is split as:
questions.explanation: Within a state, GST is shared equally as CGST and SGST. IGST applies only to inter-state sales.

questions.q: A shopkeeper sells a fan for ₹2000 (before tax) at 18% GST. How much GST does the buyer pay?
questions.explanation: 18% of 2000 = 360. This is split as CGST 9% (₹180) and SGST 9% (₹180) for an intra-state sale.

questions.q: The roots of the quadratic equation x² − 5x + 6 = 0 are:
questions.explanation: Factorise: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3. Their sum is 5 and product is 6, matching the equation.

questions.q: Solve 3x − 2 < 7 for x in the set of natural numbers. The solution is:
questions.explanation: 3x < 9 gives x < 3. Natural numbers less than 3 are 1 and 2 (natural numbers start at 1).

questions.q: A man buys ₹100 shares at ₹120 each. The company pays a 10% dividend. His dividend per share is:
questions.explanation: Dividend is always on the nominal (face) value, not the market value. 10% of ₹100 = ₹10 per share.

questions.q: The order of a matrix with 3 rows and 2 columns is:
questions.explanation: Order is always rows × columns, so 3 rows and 2 columns is 3 × 2.

questions.q: The discriminant of 2x² + 3x + 5 = 0 tells us the roots are:
questions.explanation: b² − 4ac = 9 − 40 = −31, which is negative, so the equation has no real roots.

questions.q: The mean proportional between 4 and 9 is:
questions.explanation: The mean proportional between a and b is √(ab) = √(4 × 9) = √36 = 6.

faq.q: When is the ICSE Class 10 mid-term exam usually held?
faq.a: Most CISCE-affiliated schools hold the maths mid-term between late September and mid-October. The exact date and portion are set by your school, so the circular they issue is the final word — not any online syllabus list.

faq.q: Is the mid-term paper on the full ICSE Class 10 syllabus?
faq.a: No. It covers only what has been taught by that point — usually GST, banking, shares and dividends, linear inequations, quadratic equations, ratio and proportion, and matrices. The remaining units (trigonometry, mensuration, statistics, probability) are tested in the finals.

faq.q: How many marks is the ICSE Class 10 maths mid-term?
faq.a: It is almost always set on the board pattern: 80 marks in two and a half hours, plus 15 minutes of reading time. Section A (40 marks) is compulsory; in Section B (40 marks) you attempt any four of seven questions.

faq.q: Why do I lose marks even when my final answer is correct?
faq.a: You probably skipped working. ICSE awards method marks for the formula, the substitution and each simplification step, so a right answer with no steps still loses marks. Always show every line — it is the safest way to score.
